analysis.one_liner: Starts the lobbying ban clock at term's end, closing the resign-early loophole.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have extended lobbying bans for lawmakers who resign mid-term, got zero cosponsors and died in committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, former House members cannot lobby for 1 year after leaving office and former senators for 2 years, but the clock starts the day they leave. A member who resigns mid-term can therefore finish the waiting period early and lobby while the term voters elected them to is still running. This bill would make the waiting period run from the end of the elected term instead, so quitting early to become a lobbyist no longer shortens the wait.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters. The change removes part of the financial incentive for sitting members to quit mid-term and cash in on their connections, and it puts more distance between the people who write laws and the people paid to influence them. Voters who elected someone to serve a full term would see that person's lobbying restrictions stretch to match the term they promised to serve.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting a slower revolving door

how_it_helps.text: Closes a loophole in the federal lobbying 'cooling-off' rule: instead of the ban starting when a member leaves office, it would start when the term the member was elected to expires, so resigning early can no longer shorten the wait before lobbying.

For senators, the ban would cover lobbying within 2 years after the expiration of their elected term; for House members, within 1 year after their term ends, rather than merely after they walk out the door.
The change would apply to any Senator, Representative, Delegate, or Resident Commissioner who leaves office on or after the bill's enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Sitting members of Congress who might later want to resign early and take a lobbying job — they would have to wait until their elected term expires, which for senators could be years longer than the current rule. Lobbying firms that hire former lawmakers would face a smaller pool of freshly available ex-members and longer waits for the ones who leave early.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ex-lawmakers seeking lobbying jobs and their firms

drawbacks.text: The bill applies a blunt rule: a member who resigns for an ordinary reason — health, family, a non-lobbying private-sector job — would still face a lobbying ban stretching to the end of the elected term, which for a senator who resigns early in a six-year term could mean many years of waiting.

For House members the practical effect is small, because House terms are only two years long, so the change mainly matters for senators; it would do little to slow the revolving door that already operates through ordinary end-of-term departures.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a narrow, well-targeted anti-revolving-door fix rather than a sweeping reform. It attacks one specific trick — resigning early to start the lobbying clock running — and would do most of its work for senators, whose terms are long. The cost is that early resigners for entirely innocent reasons also get a longer lobbying freeze, and House members see almost no change at all. On balance the benefit to public trust is real but modest, and the bill would not touch the much larger revolving door formed by members who serve out their terms and then lobby immediately afterward.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it quietly expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Claudia Tenney introduced the bill on April 11, 2024, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee never held a markup or vote, the bill never reached the House floor, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sitting members who might someday resign mid-term to lobby, and the lobbying firms that would have hired them, are better off: the loophole allowing the cooling-off clock to start at resignation remains open.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members eyeing lobbying careers, and lobbying firms

for.name: Rep. Claudia Tenney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill sat for the rest of the 118th Congress.

against.name: House colleagues of both parties
against.what_they_did: None signed on; the bill ended with zero cosponsors, so no bipartisan or same-party coalition formed to push it forward.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the only measurable support was the Republican sponsor, with zero cosponsors from either party.

industries.note: These firms trade on access to former lawmakers; a rule forcing early-quitting members to wait until their term expires would delay hires and shrink the pool of immediately available ex-legislators. Their gain from the current loophole comes at the cost of voters' trust in their representation.

industries.industry: Sitting members of Congress considering early resignation
industries.note: The bill extends the personal wait before a resigning member can take paid lobbying work — from departure day to the end of the elected term. Their interest in keeping the current clock runs against the public's interest in lawmakers serving out the terms voters gave them.
